lesson.title: Convenience Sampling: The Cost of Taking Who's Easy to Reach
lesson.summary: A convenience sample includes whichever individuals are easiest for the researcher to access, a non-random method that is fast and cheap but almost always biased because easy-to-reach people are rarely representative of the whole population.
lesson.body:
A convenience sample is formed by including whoever happens to be easiest to reach: shoppers near the researcher's table at a mall entrance, students walking past a particular building at a particular hour, the first 50 people to respond to an email the researcher happened to have addresses for. Nothing about the selection process involves chance; it is entirely driven by proximity and ease of access for the researcher. This is what separates a convenience sample from every genuinely random sampling method described so far, simple random, stratified, cluster, or systematic, all of which rely on some form of chance to decide who is included.

The problem is not merely theoretical. Whatever makes a group of people convenient to reach is very often correlated with the very traits a study is trying to measure, which is exactly how bias, a systematic tendency to misrepresent the population in a predictable direction, gets baked into the sample before a single question is even asked. A researcher standing outside a gym at 6 a.m. to survey attitudes toward exercise will systematically oversample people who already exercise regularly enough to be there at that hour, guaranteeing an inflated estimate of how positively the general population views exercise.

Consider a hypothetical example. A student wants to estimate what fraction of her high school supports a proposed change to the school's dress code, so she surveys the first 40 students who walk past her locker between classes. This sample is fast to collect and requires no master list or elaborate procedure, but it draws heavily from whichever students happen to have lockers, and therefore hallway traffic patterns, near hers, likely clustering by grade level, friend group, or class schedule. If dress code opinions differ by grade level, which is plausible, her convenience sample could badly misrepresent the schoolwide opinion even though 40 students is not a trivially small number.

It is worth being precise about why convenience samples fail: the issue is not sample size, a convenience sample of 5,000 people is still biased if the selection process systematically favors certain kinds of people, and no amount of additional convenient data collection fixes that underlying skew. This distinguishes bias, a systematic error in one direction that persists and even grows with more data collected the same flawed way, from ordinary sampling variability, which shrinks as sample size grows in a properly randomized sample.

Convenience sampling remains common in practice because it is cheap, fast, and requires no sampling frame, and it can be defensible for low-stakes, exploratory purposes such as pilot-testing a survey's wording before a real study. But because the sample is not the product of a chance process, standard statistical tools for estimating margins of error and confidence intervals, which are built on the mathematics of random sampling, do not apply to it in any rigorous sense. Any claim generalizing convenience sample results to a broader population should be treated with real skepticism.
